newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - Sabena vows worst over after disastrous 1996.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Sabena vows worst over after disastrous 1996.

text.p: Belgian national airline Sabena said on Wednesday that its consolidated loss more than quadrupled in 1996 but that the worst was over.

"It's obvious that the results were extremely bad but I would like you to see them within the context of a turnaround, a chapter being closed and a new chapter starting," Sabena chairman Valere Croes told a news conference.

The airline, which is 49.5 percent owned by Swissair, said it made a consolidated loss after provisions of 8.87 billion Belgian francs ($251.7 million), up from a 1.66 billion ($47 million) loss in 1995.
Exceptional charges totalled 4.1 billion francs and included a 1.5 billion franc 43 set-aside for restructuring and 1.5 billion franc fleet depreciation.
But Sabena's Swissair-appointed chief executive officer Paul Reutlinger said that the company still held on to its target of reaching break-even in 1998, and a modest loss in 1997.
He said traffic results for the first two months of 1997 had shown an encouraging 16.7 percent rise.
An extraordinary shareholders meeting would have to decide on April 24 whether to continue or halt operations at the carrier but Croes said this was just a formality.
"There is no doubt that the shareholders will decide unanimously to carry on," he said.
But the acid test would come at the end of June when Swissair would assess its cooperation with Sabena, Reutlinger said.
"1997 is the crucial year," he said. "You know the goals set by our shareholders. We have to be in line with budget in June when Swissair will make its assessment."
SAirGroup, the holding company for Swissair, said in a statement it expected Sabena to reach break even in 1998.
It said it would decide whether to write off its investment in the Belgian carrier in April.
But Reutlinger reiterated this was purely an accounting measure and did not mean that Swissair would pull out of Sabena.
He added that Sabena had no liquidity problem and was currently not considering a capital increase.
Reutlinger said that traffic in 1996 remained below par mainly due to a series of strikes early last year.
Results had been disappointing mainly on the European network and transatlantic routes registered a more encouraging performance, boosted by a closer collaboration with Delta Air.
Sabena said its cooperation with Swissair, Delta, Austrian Airlines, Virgin Express, Finnair and Tyrolean was strengthened and should show its full effect from 1997.
It said synergies with Swissair would yield 600 million each for Sabena and Swissair in 1997.
The results of synergies in general would continue to improve as the collaboration with various companies within the Swissair group increased.
"The above developments, which all derive from a radical company restructuring, should provide a firm foundation for restoring Sabena to profitability in 1998," it said.
($ = 35.24 Belgian Francs)
